Super. Human. (Channel 4, Tokyo 2020 Paralympic Games)

A bookmarkable reference page for an audio-visual advert. Section A covers media language and representation; Section B covers industries and audiences. Watch the advert first, then use the toolkit to analyse it.

ClientChannel 4 (broadcaster of the Games)
Agency4Creative, Channel 4’s in-house creative agency
DirectorBradford Young, Oscar-nominated cinematographer
ProductionSerial Pictures × Somesuch
LengthAbout 3 minutes
CampaignThird Channel 4 Paralympics campaign, with posters and social media

How to use this page

  1. Watch: view the advert, then use the frame guide to revisit key moments by timestamp.
  2. Learn: work through the Section A and Section B toolkits. Each section has a definition and an “In Super. Human.” example.
  3. Stretch: open “Going further” for the wider debates and evaluation points.
  4. Practise: use sign → denotation → connotation → underlying idea in every Section A paragraph, and link audience and industry points to evidence.

Watch the advert

Product context

  • Created to promote Channel 4’s coverage of the 2020 Tokyo Paralympic Games (held in 2021). It explores the sacrifices and trials Paralympic athletes endure in preparation.
  • Directed by Bradford Young, the Oscar-nominated cinematographer (nominated for Arrival), and devised by 4Creative.
  • Unlike earlier “Superhumans” campaigns, it focuses on the fragilities and day-to-day struggles of elite athletes, putting the emphasis on human over super.
  • Channel 4 worked with British Paralympians, and also consulted the International Paralympic Committee, the British Paralympic Association and Scope.

Frame guide

Frames are shown in full, including the video player bar, so you can see the timestamp. Times are as shown in the player and are a guide only, so check them against the video. Open the guide and note the technical, audio and visual codes at each moment.

Section A toolkit

Media language and representation

A1

Audio-visual codes

Definition

An audio-visual advert makes meaning through technical codes (camera shots, angles, movement, editing, effects), audio codes (music, dialogue, sound effects, silence), visual codes (mise-en-scène: setting, costume, props, lighting, colour) and written codes (titles and graphics). Diegetic sound belongs to the world of the film; non-diegetic sound is added, such as a soundtrack.

CodeIn Super. Human.Effect
Close-upsMany close-ups, some uncomfortable: a bruise (shown developing in time-lapse), a blister being popped, and an unfamiliar view such as a prosthetic blade being attached.Holds attention; gives intimate access to experiences audiences rarely see; makes the pain feel real.
Wide shotsTiny athletes in a huge velodrome, an empty-looking pool and gym.Connotes isolation and the scale of the challenge; the athlete works alone.
EditingCuts between gruelling routines, everyday life and cartoon moments.Juxtaposition lightens the mood and adds humour; the creatives wanted audiences to laugh as well as wince.
Colour and lightingCool, muted, naturalistic colour for training and everyday scenes, set against stylised neon dream imagery at the start.Contrasts a glamorous fantasy of success with day-to-day reality.
Mise-en-scèneGyms, pools, a velodrome, home, a café; a bucket labelled “Mr Puke Bucket”; medical settings and props.Shows the unglamorous reality of elite sport and life as a disabled athlete.
Music (non-diegetic)“So You Want To Be a Boxer” from Bugsy Malone, a recognisable, upbeat, stirring tune.Connotes struggle and hard work paying off; ironic contrast with the painful images; familiar to older audiences.
Sound effects (diegetic)Heavy breathing and grunting, juxtaposed with everyday sounds such as a woman in childbirth and a baby crying.Connotes effort and the ordinary human experiences athletes also go through.
Written codes and effectsThe title “Super. Human.” appears; “Super” shatters like glass, leaving “Human”.Visually enacts the campaign idea: the superhero label breaks.
Absence of voice-overNo narration and no graphics moralising about disability; the stories are shown.Realism and authenticity; audiences draw their own conclusions.
Exam move

Name the technique, quote or describe the moment, then explain the effect on the audience and link to the idea. For example: “The extreme close-up of the bruise connotes the physical cost of training, which supports the advert’s idea that these athletes are human, not superheroes.”

A2

Narrative and Barthes’ codes Barthes

Definition

Narrative is how events are ordered to tell a story. Barthes’ codes describe how texts create meaning: hermeneutic (enigma), proairetic (action and tension), semantic (connotation), symbolic (larger themes and oppositions) and cultural (shared knowledge).

In Super. Human.: narrative structure
  1. Dream: the advert opens inside the dream of Paralympic gold medallist Kadeena Cox, in neon-tunnel imagery.
  2. Rupture: a starting pistol shakes her out of the dream and reality bites. Your notes describe the dream sequence being shattered at the beginning.
  3. Montage: a sequence of training, pain, setbacks, home life and humour across several athletes.
  4. Return to the dream (around the two-minute mark): we return to Cox’s subconscious, where she imagines outpacing a bronze-medal finish on the track.
  5. Payoff: “To be a Paralympian there’s got to be something wrong with you,” as “Super” shatters, leaving “Human”.
CodeIn Super. Human.
HermeneuticThe closing line poses an enigma: what is “wrong” with a Paralympian? The shattering title answers: nothing is wrong with them; they are human.
ProaireticThe starting pistol, the montage of repeated efforts and the rising pace of the song build tension and expectation towards a race and a result.
SemanticBlood, bruises and a blister connote pain; the bucket connotes exhaustion and sacrifice; the wheelchair at the café connotes exclusion.
SymbolicSuper / human; dream / reality; glory / pain. Shattering glass symbolises breaking a stereotype.
CulturalAudiences know Channel 4’s earlier Paralympic adverts and the Bugsy Malone song. One Channel 4 presenter compared waiting for the advert every four years to the John Lewis Christmas advert.
A3

Reading the images: working alone, suffering, no help?

Definition

When you analyse a moving-image text, group moments by theme and explain how codes build it. Your class notes organise the advert under working alone, suffering and no help?

Working alone
  • Evidence: the athlete alone in the gym (0:41), the tiny figure in the pool (0:52), the cyclist on an indoor trainer (1:25) and the small rider in the velodrome (1:40).
  • Codes: wide shots dwarf the athletes; cool, empty spaces; little or no dialogue.
  • Idea: elite sport is lonely, repetitive work. Success is built in private.
Suffering
  • Evidence: the fallen rider (1:45), the bruise (1:47), the needle and blister (1:48), the bucket (1:30) and the visceral montage (2:30).
  • Codes: extreme close-ups, time-lapse, bodily imagery and heavy breathing. The bouncy soundtrack contrasts with the pain.
  • Idea: the physical cost of success; the athletes are fragile, not invincible. This is a deliberate shock tactic.
No help?
  • Evidence: the wheelchair wheel (1:48) and the café sequence (1:50 to 1:51), in which rugby player Kylie Grimes is unable to enter a café because of access issues, according to your notes. The video call (1:14) shows loved ones at a distance.
  • Codes: low-level close-ups of the wheel on rough ground; the café seen from outside, with people already inside.
  • Idea: beyond training, society itself creates barriers. The advert asks audiences to notice them.
A4

Binary oppositions Lévi-StraussA Level

Definition

Claude Lévi-Strauss argued that texts make meaning through binary oppositions, pairs of opposites understood by contrast. Often the text asks us to value one side, or to challenge the opposition itself.

OppositionWhere it appearsWhat the advert does with it
Super / HumanThe title and the final shattering of “Super”Chooses “human” and rejects the superhero stereotype.
Dream / realityNeon dream at the start and its return, against gritty training scenesShows that glory is built on hard, painful reality.
Glory / painThe upbeat song against bruises, blisters and bucketConnects success and suffering rather than hiding the suffering.
Humour / seriousnessCartoon and bucket jokes against gruelling effortHumour makes serious content engaging and avoids pity.
Alone / supportedLone training against the video call and the inaccessible caféAsks who helps, and who or what stands in the way.
Disabled / non-disabledAthletes’ everyday experiences set alongside universal ones such as childbirth and a baby cryingChallenges the opposition by showing shared human experience.
A5

Intertextuality and conventions

Definition

Intertextuality is when a text refers to other texts, building meaning from audience knowledge. Conventions are the expected features of a form or genre; texts may follow, subvert or challenge them.

In Super. Human.
  • Bugsy Malone: “So You Want To Be a Boxer” is borrowed from the 1976 musical film. Its cheerful, comic tone is set against the grim images.
  • Previous campaigns: this is the third Paralympics campaign from Channel 4, following the 2012 and 2016 “Superhumans” adverts. Audiences expect a big, event-like film, and the new advert deliberately changes the earlier approach.
  • Conventions of charity and awareness adverts: these typically use serious voice-overs and focus on disability. Super. Human. avoids the voice-over and the moralising graphics.
  • Sports adverts: training montages and slow-motion glory shots are conventional; here the montage shows pain and humour instead.
A6

Representation of disability HallGauntlett

Definition

For Stuart Hall, representation is the construction of meaning through selection and combination. Stereotypes reduce groups to a few fixed traits; countertypes challenge them; shared conceptual maps develop through repeated representations. David Gauntlett argues identities are built from the role models and representations media offer.

In Super. Human.: challenging two stereotypes
  • The victim: the advert does not present the athletes as objects of pity. There is no sad music or voice-over, and humour keeps control with the athletes.
  • The superhero: earlier campaigns presented disabled people as superheroes. The creatives said that felt right at the time but did not tell the full story. Here the athletes are “flawed and vulnerable” like everyone, and “Super” literally breaks.
  • Selection: private, uncomfortable, ordinary moments are chosen. Combination: pain with humour, effort with everyday life.
  • Shared conceptual map: the campaign aims to shift how audiences think about disability, treating disabled athletes as elite sportspeople who happen to face extra barriers.
  • Gauntlett: real athletes become relatable role models. 4Creative reported a young boy tweeting that he wanted to be a Paralympian when he grew up, which suggests an audience member building an identity from the representation.
Extending the analysis A Level
  • van Zoonen (gender): women and men appear as athletes first. Ask how far women are represented differently from the men, and how far the advert challenges gender stereotypes as well as disability stereotypes.
  • bell hooks (intersectionality): identity combines gender, race, class and disability. Ask whether the advert shows a range of people, and whose experiences (for example, ethnicity or class) might be less visible.
  • Gilroy (otherness): disabled people are often positioned as “other” in media. Ask how the advert tries to remove that distance by showing universal experiences.
Section B toolkit

Media industries and audiences

B1

Industries: Channel 4, regulation and funding

Definition

Curran & Seaton: who owns and funds media affects what is produced. Livingstone & Lunt: regulation, and audiences as citizens or consumers. Hesmondhalgh: cultural industries reduce risk by repeating proven formulas, brands and sequels.

In Super. Human.
  • Public service remit: Channel 4 is publicly owned and funded by advertising. Its remit includes appealing to the tastes and interests of a culturally diverse society (Ofcom). Promoting the Paralympics fits this remit.
  • In-house agency: 4Creative produced the idea, so Channel 4 promotes its own coverage, building the brand as well as the event. The Chief Marketing Officer said the Paralympics had been treated as an afterthought of the Olympics, and this campaign aimed to put it on an equal footing.
  • Hesmondhalgh (risk minimisation): the third in a successful series, with a trusted brand idea (“Superhumans”) and a respected director, but with a fresh angle to avoid repeating itself.
  • Regulation: Ofcom is the UK communications regulator, which oversees Channel 4’s licence and public service remit. Advertising content is also regulated by the ASA (Advertising Standards Authority), the other regulator, which applies the advertising codes. Shock tactics such as the blister must stay within these rules.
  • Citizen or consumer? The advert addresses audiences as citizens (invited to rethink disability) and as consumers (invited to watch Channel 4’s coverage).
B2

Targeting, reaching and addressing the audience

Definition

The target audience is the group a producer aims to reach. Mode of address is how the text speaks to them. Producers also use personalisation, unique selling points (USPs) and shock tactics to gain attention.

In Super. Human.
  • Target audience: a broad group: Channel 4 viewers, who largely fall into the 16 to 34 age bracket; sports fans; and viewers who want more inclusive representations of social groups.
  • Personalisation: real, human stories about the day-to-day struggles of being a disabled athlete in training encourage audiences to identify with them.
  • Technical codes: close-ups, some uncomfortable, and unfamiliar views hold attention; cartoons lighten the mood through humour.
  • Audio codes: the familiar Bugsy Malone song grabs attention; older audiences know the film. Struggle sounds are juxtaposed with everyday sounds.
  • USP: the “showing” of the athletes’ stories, with no voice-over or moralising graphics and a realistic portrayal.
  • Mode of address: mostly indirect, as we observe the athletes; the closing line speaks directly to the audience’s own assumptions.
  • Social context: it addresses the under-representation of disabled athletes in mainstream media and presents athletes as neither victims nor heroes.
B3

Reception and effects HallGerbnerBandura

Definition

Hall’s reception theory: audiences decode in preferred, negotiated or oppositional ways. Gerbner’s cultivation theory: long-term repeated exposure shapes beliefs. Bandura: people learn by observing and imitating role models.

TheoryApplied to Super. Human.
Hall: preferredThe upbeat soundtrack, personalisation and positive representations encourage viewers to accept Channel 4’s intended meaning. Real athletes create a preferred reading: invest in their stories and watch the Paralympics.
Hall: negotiatedSome viewers acknowledge the advert’s legitimacy but feel distanced from the sporting theme, while becoming more open to examining their misconceptions about disability.
Hall: oppositionalPossible from those who do not support Channel 4’s ethos of representing marginalised groups, older viewers, non-regular Channel 4 viewers, or those uninterested in sport.
GerbnerAudiences may have become desensitised to awareness-raising adverts through repeated exposure to conventional codes such as serious voice-overs about disability. This advert challenges Gerbner’s idea by offering a fresh perspective that encourages viewers to question assumptions.
BanduraRealistic athlete role models may be imitated or admired, as in the boy’s tweet that he wanted to become a Paralympian.
Audience reception

The advert deliberately challenges viewers with shock tactics: the time-lapse bruise, the blister popping, and an athlete unable to enter a café due to access issues. The provocative line “To be a Paralympian there’s got to be something wrong with you” invites viewers to examine their language around disability and reframe their perceptions positively.

B4

Reach, digital audiences and success JenkinsShirky

Definition

Jenkins: participatory culture, where audiences take part in, remix and discuss media. Shirky: digital tools make audiences into producers and sharers (prosumers), the “end of the audience”.

In Super. Human.
  • Reach: Channel 4’s Paralympic coverage was viewed by 20 million people, a third of the UK population, with a fifth of 16 to 34-year-olds. The marketing campaign reached 81% of the UK population.
  • Digital: the campaign included posters and social media. #C4paralympics generated 4.1 million TikTok views, there were 2.6 million streams on All 4, and Channel 4 reported half a billion global impressions from @C4Paralympics tweets.
  • Participation: audiences can react, share and reply online, so the advert becomes part of a wider conversation (Jenkins, Shirky).
  • Evaluation: reach figures show it was seen widely, but they do not prove attitudes changed. Compare with the evidence on effects in B3.
Going further

The wider debates

From “Superhumans” to “Super. Human.”: a shifting conceptual map

Channel 4’s earlier Paralympics adverts challenged the idea of disabled people as victims by presenting athletes as superheroes. Their creators later said that approach was right at the time but did not tell the full story. Super. Human. moves the representation on again: ordinary people doing extraordinary things, in pain and with humour.

Using Hall: representations can shift a shared conceptual map over time. Using Gauntlett: each campaign provides different identities to pick from. This helps you argue that representation is not fixed, and that today’s countertype can become tomorrow’s convention.

Links: Hall · Gauntlett · Gerbner (does repetition of “inspiration” messages blunt their effect?)

Linking Section A and Section B in one answer

Strong responses connect media language to audience and industry ideas. For example: the absence of voice-over (media language) supports the USP of “showing” (audience targeting), which suits Channel 4’s remit to appeal to a culturally diverse society (industries) and encourages a negotiated or preferred reading (Hall).

Links: Barthes · Hall · Livingstone & Lunt · Hesmondhalgh

Identity: Gauntlett and the athletes as role models

Gauntlett’s idea of “pick and mix” identity treats media as a resource. Real athletes with names, stories and flaws offer a richer set of identities than a symbolic “hero” or “victim” figure. Compare Tide, where one narrow identity is offered, and Kiss of the Vampire, where older and newer identities are mixed.

Evaluation points for exam answers

  • Does it avoid stereotypes entirely? “Human” may replace “superhero” with another narrow picture: suffering. Ask whether the focus on pain risks reinforcing pity.
  • Whose voice? The agency and director worked with athletes and organisations such as Scope. Consider whose perspective shaped the advert and how far disabled people controlled the representation.
  • Purpose and profit: it is also marketing for Channel 4’s coverage. An advert can challenge stereotypes and serve commercial interests at once.
  • Reach versus effect: a third of the UK saw the coverage, but reach is not the same as changed attitudes.
  • Shock tactics: do they engage audiences or risk alienating some (oppositional readings)?
  • Reception theory: use specific groups (for example regular Channel 4 viewers, sports fans, older audiences) to justify preferred, negotiated or oppositional readings.

Applying the ideas

Super. Human.: sign → denotation → connotation → underlying idea

SignDenotationConnotationUnderlying idea
“Super” shattering (2:51)Glass cracks over the title; “Super” breaks awayBreaking a false image; fragilityRejecting the superhero stereotype; “human” as the preferred identity (Hall, Lévi-Strauss).
Time-lapse bruise (1:47)Extreme close-up of a bruise formingPain, cost, vulnerabilityAthletes are human; shock tactic aids reception (Hall, Barthes semantic code).

Extra example 1: Tide (1950s print advert) Section A

SignDenotation / connotationUnderlying idea
“Tide’s got what women want!”Confident headline; speaks for all womenTells the audience what to think. Anchorage and direct address (Barthes).
Smiling woman hugging the boxDevotion to the productReinforces a stereotype (Hall); one narrow identity (Gauntlett).
Compare: Tide tells women what they want, using a headline and commands. Super. Human. shows and lets the audience draw conclusions. Which approach gives audiences more freedom to decode (Hall)?

Extra example 2: Kiss of the Vampire (1963 poster) Section A

SignDenotation / connotationUnderlying idea
Woman on her knees, throat bareSubmission and vulnerabilityReinforces the victim stereotype (Hall).
Woman holding a kneeling manPower and dominanceA countertype reflecting its time (Gauntlett, van Zoonen).
Compare: both challenge a stereotype but in different ways. A horror poster mixes a countertype with older conventions; a public-service broadcaster’s advert builds its entire message around rejecting two stereotypes. How do industry purpose and audience shape this?

Connections

Across the course

This text is studied for both sections, so it links closely to other set texts.

  • Section A links: Tide (an advert that tells women what they want) and Kiss of the Vampire (stereotypes and countertypes) give contrasting approaches to representation.
  • Film: I, Daniel Blake and Black Panther also represent groups often under-represented in mainstream media. Compare how each text and its industry context handles this.
  • Public service media: compare Channel 4’s remit with BBC Radio 4’s Woman’s Hour or the Have You Heard George’s Podcast? and how each addresses audiences as citizens and consumers.
  • Newspapers: compare how the Daily Mirror and The Times (1 Feb 2022) address their audiences and represent groups, using the same preferred, negotiated and oppositional framework.
  • Digital audiences: compare campaign engagement here with fandom and participation around Assassin’s Creed (Jenkins, Shirky).
